findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

alternatives: NSAID (naproxen 500 mg or ibuprofen 400 mg) with an antiemetic at headache onset, with the gastrointestinal bleeding caution above
contraindications: Sumatriptan with MAO inhibitors (and within 2 weeks of stopping one), and with ergotamine within 24 h.
Sumatriptan (SmPC): ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura.
interactions: Sumatriptan with sertraline: both serotonergic. The FDA 2006 alert cites a risk of serotonin syndrome; the American Headache Society position paper (Evans RW et al., Headache 2010;50:1089-1099) found the evidence insufficient to restrict co-prescription, and a cohort of co-prescribed patients (Orlova Y et al., JAMA Neurol 2018;75:566-572) found serotonin syndrome rare (about 0.6 to 2.3 cases per 10,000 person-years). Co-prescription is acceptable with counselling.
Sertraline with NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding; consider gastroprotection if an NSAID is used often.
Sertraline with amitriptyline: sertraline inhibits CYP2D6 and can raise tricyclic levels; additive serotonergic effect. Use a low tricyclic dose with monitoring if combined.
output.proposed: sumatriptan 50 mg as needed with sertraline 50 mg daily
output.summary: Serotonergic combination with a low observed risk of serotonin syndrome; co-prescription acceptable with counselling. Sources: FDA alert 2006; AHS position paper 2010; Orlova 2018; sumatriptan and sertraline SmPC.
warnings: Counsel on the features of serotonin toxicity (agitation, tremor, myoclonus or clonus, sweating, fever, tachycardia) and to seek care if they occur.
Avoid adding further serotonergic drugs (tramadol, St John's wort, linezolid, other antidepressants) without review.
Triptans are taken at the onset of headache, not during the aura. Use on 10 or more days a month risks medication-overuse headache.
Topiramate and candesartan have no pharmacokinetic interaction with sertraline; topiramate requires the pregnancy prevention programme in women who can become pregnant.

output.query: triptan SSRI co-prescription serotonin syndrome risk evidence

results.finding: The case reports behind the 2006 FDA alert seldom met the Hunter criteria; the available evidence does not support limiting the use of triptans with SSRIs or SNRIs, though vigilance is advised.
results.source: Evans RW, Tepper SJ, Shapiro RE, Sun-Edelstein C, Tietjen GE. The FDA alert on serotonin syndrome with use of triptans combined with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: American Headache Society position paper. Headache 2010;50:1089-1099

results.finding: In a large health-system cohort of patients co-prescribed a triptan and an SSRI or SNRI, serotonin syndrome was rare, with an estimated incidence of 0.6 to 2.3 cases per 10,000 person-years of exposure.
results.source: Orlova Y, Rizzoli P, Loder E. Association of coprescription of triptan antimigraine drugs and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressants with serotonin syndrome. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:566-572

output.summary: Serotonin syndrome with triptan plus SSRI or SNRI co-prescription is rare; the AHS does not advise against the combination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four stereotyped attacks of right-field visual then right perioral sensory aura over 20-25 min followed by headache; 6 of 6 C characteristics; normal examination; no serotonin toxicity features
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and SNNOOP10 red-flag review, applying each ICHD-3 1.2 criterion
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with aura is a clinical diagnosis. The history establishes four typical attacks (ICHD-3 1.2.1), documents the medication timeline that worries her, and screens for the red flags that would justify imaging; none is present beyond a typical new-onset aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, haemorrhage or mass; a few punctate non-specific white matter foci
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI (not needed for a typical aura with a normal examination)
action_criteria.rationale: Optional: a typical aura with a normal examination needs no imaging (AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336; AAN Choosing Wisely). Punctate white matter hyperintensities are common in migraine with aura and do not change management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Triptan with SSRI is serotonergic but serotonin syndrome is rare; continue both with counselling; avoid adding other serotonergic drugs
action_criteria.label: Check sumatriptan against sertraline (serotonin syndrome question) and the options for further treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Required: the patient takes sertraline and sumatriptan together and asks about the interaction; the check decides whether the effective acute treatment continues. The FDA 2006 alert is weighed against the AHS 2010 position paper and the 2018 cohort data.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on the observed rate of serotonin syndrome with triptan plus SSRI
action_criteria.label: Literature on triptan and SSRI co-prescription
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not stop sumatriptan or call it contraindicated because she takes sertraline.
Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Explain the diagnosis: migraine with typical visual and sensory aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); the normal examination and typical features need no further tests.

Continue sumatriptan with sertraline, with counselling: the combination is serotonergic but serotonin syndrome is rare (AHS 2010 position paper); she should seek care for agitation, tremor, clonus, sweating or fever, and avoid adding other serotonergic drugs such as tramadol or St John's wort.
Take sumatriptan at headache onset, not during the aura, and on fewer than 10 days a month (medication-overuse risk).

Answer her question about sertraline: the predisposition predates it (father's and sister's migraine, earlier brief visual episodes); continuing it is reasonable if the depression is responding, and any change is agreed with her prescriber rather than made abruptly.

Keep a headache diary; prevention is not indicated at about one attack a month (AHS 2021); if attacks become more frequent, choose a preventive compatible with sertraline and her depression (for example candesartan, only with reliable contraception as it is contraindicated in pregnancy; topiramate only under the pregnancy prevention programme).

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its primary migraine end points in PREMIUM, PRIMA or MIST.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

accepted: Migraine with visual and somatosensory aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); likely genetically predisposed migraine unmasked by sertraline; sertraline-sumatriptan co-administration acceptable with counselling

differential.key_features: Requires neuromuscular, autonomic and mental status features (Hunter criteria); she has none after sumatriptan doses, and the observed risk of the combination is low.
Positive visual then sensory symptoms spreading over 20-25 minutes, followed by headache, in four stereotyped attacks at 38 without vascular risk factors are features of aura.
Current attacks are homonymous (right field) with right perioral tingling, not monocular; the earlier brief flashes had no headache and their monocularity was never confirmed.
Occipital seizures give brief, often coloured circular phenomena; a spreading crescent over 20-25 minutes with a march to the face and migrainous headache is typical of aura.
Episodic attacks with complete recovery, no daily headache, no papilloedema.

key_clinical_evidence: Four stereotyped attacks with visual then sensory aura and headache meet ICHD-3 1.2.1.
Family history and earlier brief visual episodes show the migraine predisposition predates sertraline.
Triptan plus SSRI: serotonin syndrome is rare; the AHS 2010 position paper does not advise against co-prescription, and counselling is enough.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Her father's and sister's migraine and the earlier brief visual episodes show a predisposition that predates sertraline; the attacks meet migraine with typical aura whatever the trigger.
red_herrings.data_point: Aura onset 2 weeks after starting sertraline
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on sertraline as the cause of the attacks and lead to stopping an effective antidepressant

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The FDA alert rests on case reports that seldom met serotonin syndrome criteria; the observed risk is low and co-prescription with counselling is acceptable.
red_herrings.data_point: Sertraline with sumatriptan in a pharmacist aware of the FDA alert
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead to calling the triptan contraindicated and withdrawing effective acute treatment

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A few punctate frontal subcortical foci are common and non-specific in migraine with aura; with a normal examination and no relevant family history they need no further investigation.
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt a demyelination, vasculitis or CADASIL work-up

findings.result: Four stereotyped attacks in 3 months, the first 2 weeks after sertraline was started. Before that, a few brief (5-10 min) flashes of light over 2-3 years without headache, which she attributed to one eye; monocularity was never checked by covering each eye.

Visual: shimmering crescent in the right visual field (positive, unilateral). Sensory: tingling of the right lips and chin starting while the visual disturbance spreads (positive, unilateral, in succession). No speech, motor, brainstem or retinal symptoms.
Visual disturbance expands over 20-25 min; all aura symptoms resolve within about 30 min.
Follows the aura within minutes: left-sided, pulsating, 8/10, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, lasting 8-12 h. Sumatriptan 50 mg effective.

Sertraline 50 mg daily for 4 months; sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for 6 weeks, about one attack a month. No symptoms of serotonin toxicity (no agitation, tremor, myoclonus, sweating or fever) after doses.
Normal neurological examination between attacks: full visual fields, no papilloedema, normal facial sensation. BP 120/76 mmHg.

New headache pattern in the last 3 months: present (onset at 38, typical aura features). Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, deficit outside the aura, thunderclap onset, onset over 50, positional or Valsalva features, papilloedema, pregnancy, painful eye, trauma and medication overuse: absent.
Father had headaches with visual flashing in his 40s; sister has migraine. No hemiplegic migraine or stroke.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. Four attacks fulfilling ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A-D with 6 of 6 C characteristics: migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), visual and sensory aura with headache. 2. Normal interictal examination. 3. No clinical features of serotonin toxicity.

additional_observations: Indication: new-onset visual and sensory aura at 38.
Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, FLAIR, DWI with ADC and SWI.
No infarct, haemorrhage, mass or abnormal susceptibility. Ventricles and sulci normal for age.

findings.location: frontal subcortical white matter, scattered (four foci)

mri.impression: 1. Four punctate non-specific frontal subcortical white matter hyperintensities. 2. No acute infarct, haemorrhage or mass.

patient.chief_complaint: New right-sided visual disturbance, lip tingling, and headache — 4 episodes over 3 months, started with new antidepressant

family_history: Father had 'headaches with visual flashing' in 40s; sister has migraines; no family history of stroke, hemiplegic migraine, or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Pharmacist; divorced; two children; non-smoker; 4-6 units alcohol/week; no illicit drugs; professional knowledge of drug interactions

patient.history_present_illness:
A 38-year-old Lebanese-Australian woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic with four similar episodes over the past 3 months. Each episode begins with shimmering, crescent-shaped visual disturbance in the right visual field that expands over approximately 20-25 minutes, often accompanied by tingling of the right side of her lips and chin. After the visual and sensory symptoms resolve, she develops a severe left-sided pulsating headache (8/10) with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, lasting 8-12 hours.

She had never experienced similar episodes prior to starting sertraline 50 mg for depression 4 months ago. The first aura episode occurred 2 weeks after starting sertraline. She is concerned about whether the antidepressant caused these episodes. She has a personal history of depression (not previously treated with medication) and anxiety. Her sister also has migraines. She is also taking sumatriptan 50 mg for headaches, prescribed by her GP 6 weeks ago, with good acute effect. She is not on oral contraceptives (divorced, no need for contraception). Non-smoker.

On closer questioning, she reports that her father had similar 'headaches with visual flashing' in his 40s. She also reports that she has experienced mild, brief (5-10 minute) flashes of light in one eye on a few occasions over the past 2-3 years that she dismissed as eye strain — she never consulted about these.
